Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2

R
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Tutorial
A step-by-step guide to evolving a basic density plot into an advanced, publication-ready visualization
Author

Your Name

Published

October 14, 2025

Introduction

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated density plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Density plots are excellent for visualizing the distribution of continuous variables, showing the probability density function and revealing patterns like skewness, modality, and concentration of values.

We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: focus on diamonds with standard cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"),
         carat <= 3) %>%                           # Remove extreme outliers
  mutate(cut = factor(cut, levels = c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", 
                                      "Premium", "Ideal")))  # Set factor order

# Preview the data
head(data_diamonds)
# A tibble: 6 × 10

  <dbl> <ord>     <ord> <ord>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>

Chart 1: Basic Density Plot

Let’s start with a simple density plot showing the distribution of diamond carat weights.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_density()                          # Create density plot

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping carat weight to the x-axis

Line 2: geom_density() - Adds a density curve showing the smoothed probability distribution of carat values

What we have so far: A functional but basic density plot. The distribution shape is visible but the chart lacks context, comparative groups, and visual refinement.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll improve the chart by comparing multiple groups, adding fill colors, adjusting transparency, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Multiple density curves comparing different cut qualities
  • Color fill with transparency to show overlapping distributions
  • Improved axis labels and title for clarity
  • Clean theme to remove visual clutter
  • Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
  • Formatted x-axis for better readability
ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic by cut
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +                             # Density with transparency
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                   # Apply color palette
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) +      # Set x-axis breaks
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Diamond Carat Weight by Cut Quality",  # Main title
    subtitle = "Higher quality cuts tend toward smaller carat sizes",  # Subtitle
    x = "Carat Weight",                                   # X-axis label
    y = "Density",                                        # Y-axis label
    fill = "Cut Quality"                                  # Legend title
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), # Bold title
    legend.position = "top"                               # Move legend to top
  )

Code Explanation

Line 1: aes(x = carat, fill = cut) - Maps carat weight to x-axis and cut quality to fill color, enabling comparison across groups

Line 2: geom_density(alpha = 0.6) - Creates overlapping density curves with 60% opacity to show where distributions intersect

Line 3: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer

Line 4: scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) - Sets regular x-axis breaks every 0.5 carats for easier reading

Lines 5-11: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing insight, axis labels, and legend title for context

Line 12: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements

Lines 13-16: theme() - Customizes title formatting and moves legend to top for better space utilization

What we have now: A much more informative chart showing how carat distributions differ across cut qualities. The transparent overlays and clean formatting make comparisons easy, revealing that ideal cuts concentrate in smaller carat ranges.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s take it to the next level with ridge-style presentation, statistical annotations, enhanced colors, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Stacked density presentation for clearer group comparison
  • Statistical reference lines showing means for each group
  • Sample size annotations in legend
  • Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
  • Enhanced typography with refined spacing
  • Rug plot showing individual observations
  • Data source caption for proper attribution
  • Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance
# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
cut_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    mean_carat = mean(carat),                      # Mean carat
    median_carat = median(carat),                  # Median carat
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly gradient)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#D55E00",                              # Orange-red for lowest
  "Good" = "#E69F00",                              # Orange
  "Very Good" = "#F0E442",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#009E73",                           # Green
  "Ideal" = "#0072B2"                              # Blue for highest
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut, color = cut)) +
  # Main density curves
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Add rug plot showing individual observations (sampled to avoid overplotting)
  geom_rug(data = data_diamonds %>% 
             group_by(cut) %>% 
             slice_sample(prop = 0.01),
           alpha = 0.3, length = unit(0.02, "npc")) +
  # Add mean reference lines
  geom_vline(data = cut_summary,
             aes(xintercept = mean_carat, color = cut),
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7,
             alpha = 0.8) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_colors,
                    name = "Cut Quality",
                    labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                   " (n = ", 
                                   format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                   ")")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cut_colors,
                     name = "Cut Quality",
                     labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                    " (n = ", 
                                    format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                    ")")) +
  # Format x-axis with better breaks and labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.25),
                     labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))) +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Carat Distribution Reveals Quality-Size Trade-offs",
    subtitle = "Ideal cut diamonds concentrate around 0.5-1.0 carats, while lower grades show broader distributions\nDashed lines indicate mean values for each cut quality",
    x = "Carat Weight",
    y = "Probability Density",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset (53,940 diamonds) | Sample of 1% shown in rug plot | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for interpretation
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 2.5,
           label = "Ideal cuts peak\nat lower carats",
           size = 3.5, fontface = "italic",
           color = "gray30", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("curve", x = 2.3, y = 2.4, 
           xend = 1.2, yend = 3.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = -0.3, color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )

Code Explanation

Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes, means, and medians for each cut category, used for annotations and legend labels

Lines 12-19: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low quality) to cool (high quality) colors, optimized for colorblind accessibility

Line 21: ggplot() initializes the plot with carat mapped to x-axis and cut quality mapped to both fill and color (for consistency)

Lines 23-24: geom_density() creates density curves with transparency and thicker lines for better visibility

Lines 25-29: geom_rug() adds small tick marks at the bottom showing individual data points (sampled to 1% to avoid overplotting)

Lines 30-35: geom_vline() adds dashed vertical lines at the mean carat value for each cut quality, color-coded by group

Lines 37-48: scale_fill_manual() and scale_color_manual() apply our custom color palette and enhance legend labels with sample sizes in parentheses

Lines 50-52: scale_x_continuous() sets fine-grained breaks (every 0.25 carats) with proper decimal formatting

Line 54: scale_y_continuous() expands the top slightly to prevent clipping

Lines 56-62: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells a story, multi-line subtitle with interpretation guidance, and detailed caption with attribution and methodology notes

Lines 64-71: annotate() adds a text annotation with an arrow pointing to the Ideal cut peak, helping guide interpretation

Lines 72-99: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend positioned at bottom with custom sizing - Grid customization with lighter lines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that clearly communicates how diamond carat distributions vary by cut quality. The combination of overlapping density curves, mean reference lines, rug plot, and interpretive annotations creates a comprehensive and accessible chart suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s a side-by-side view of our progression:

Aspect Basic Intermediate Advanced
Readability Poor (single curve, no context) Good (multiple groups, colored) Excellent (all + means + annotations)
Context None Title & subtitle added Full context with interpretation guide
Visual Appeal Plain gray curve Multiple colored curves Multi-layered + custom palette + rug
Data Layers Density only Density curves Density + rug + mean lines + annotation
Statistical Info Distribution shape only Multiple distributions Added means, sample sizes, interpretation

Key Takeaways

Tip

Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Density Plots:

  1. Adjust bandwidth carefully - Use the adjust parameter in geom_density() (default = 1) to control smoothness. Lower values show more detail, higher values create smoother curves

  2. Use transparency for overlaps - Set alpha between 0.5-0.7 when comparing multiple groups to show where distributions intersect

  3. Add rug plots strategically - For datasets with <1,000 points per group, show all observations. For larger datasets, sample 1-5% with slice_sample()

  4. Show reference statistics - Add vertical lines for means, medians, or other important values using geom_vline()

  5. Consider the y-axis - Density values can be unintuitive; consider adding “Probability Density” to the label to clarify meaning

  6. Color with purpose - Use color gradients that match the ordering or meaning of your categories

  7. Handle long tails - For highly skewed data, consider log-transforming the x-axis with scale_x_log10()

  8. Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per group in the legend or plot

  9. Choose appropriate alternatives - For discrete data or small samples (<30), consider histograms or violin plots instead

  10. Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other distribution visualizations:

  • Ridge plots (via ggridges) for comparing many distributions vertically
  • Violin plots for combining density with box plot statistics
  • Histograms for showing actual counts rather than smoothed densities
  • Empirical cumulative distribution functions for showing percentiles

Want to create faceted density plots?

You can split by additional variables using faceting:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ color, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Carat Distribution by Cut and Color",
       x = "Carat Weight",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

This creates separate density plots for each diamond color, still showing cut quality comparisons within each panel.

## Introduction

In this tutorial, we'll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated density plots using `ggplot2`. We'll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Density plots are excellent for visualizing the distribution of continuous variables, showing the probability density function and revealing patterns like skewness, modality, and concentration of values.

We'll use the built-in `diamonds` dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

## Setup

First, let's load the required packages and prepare our data:

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: focus on diamonds with standard cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"),
```

## Chart 1: Basic Density Plot

Let's start with a simple density plot showing the distribution of diamond carat weights.

```{r}
#| label: chart-basic
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_density()                          # Create density plot
```

### Code Explanation

**Line 1:** `ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat))` - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping carat weight to the x-axis

**Line 2:** `geom_density()` - Adds a density curve showing the smoothed probability distribution of carat values

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**What we have so far:**
A functional but basic density plot. The distribution shape is visible but the chart lacks context, comparative groups, and visual refinement.
:::

## Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we'll improve the chart by comparing multiple groups, adding fill colors, adjusting transparency, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

- **Improved axis labels** and title for clarity

```{r}
#| label: chart-intermediate

#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic by cut
```

## Key Takeaways

::: {.callout-tip}
**Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Density Plots:**

1. **Adjust bandwidth carefully** - Use the `adjust` parameter in `geom_density()` (default = 1) to control smoothness. Lower values show more detail, higher values create smoother curves

2. **Use transparency for overlaps** - Set `alpha` between 0.5-0.7 when comparing multiple groups to show where distributions intersect

3. **Add rug plots strategically** - For datasets with <1,000 points per group, show all observations. For larger datasets, sample 1-5% with `slice_sample()`

4. **Show reference statistics** - Add vertical lines for means, medians, or other important values using `geom_vline()`

5. **Consider the y-axis** - Density values can be unintuitive; consider adding "Probability Density" to the label to clarify meaning

6. **Color with purpose** - Use color gradients that match the ordering or meaning of your categories

7. **Handle long tails** - For highly skewed data, consider log-transforming the x-axis with `scale_x_log10()`

8. **Annotate sample sizes** - Always show the number of observations per group in the legend or plot

9. **Choose appropriate alternatives** - For discrete data or small samples (<30), consider histograms or violin plots instead

10. **Export at high resolution** - Use `ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)` for publication-quality images

:::

---

## Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other distribution visualizations:

- **Ridge plots** (via `ggridges`) for comparing many distributions vertically
- **Violin plots** for combining density with box plot statistics
- **Histograms** for showing actual counts rather than smoothed densities
- **Empirical cumulative distribution functions** for showing percentiles

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**Want to create faceted density plots?**

You can split by additional variables using faceting:

```r
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ color, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Carat Distribution by Cut and Color",
       x = "Carat Weight",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

This creates separate density plots for each diamond color, still showing cut quality comparisons within each panel.
:::
